sections.body:
**Preload** is the degree of myocardial stretch at the end of diastole - the load on the muscle *before* it contracts. Strictly it is the **end-diastolic sarcomere length**; because we cannot measure that clinically, we approximate it with (in descending order of fidelity): **LV end-diastolic volume (LVEDV)** -> **LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP)** -> **pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP/PAWP)** -> central venous pressure.

More stretch -> more forceful contraction (the **Frank-Starling** mechanism). Preload is therefore the input the ventricle converts into stroke volume.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Preload is set by how much blood returns to and fills the ventricle in diastole - i.e. by **venous return** and diastolic filling time.

Determinants that **raise** preload: increased blood/intravascular volume, increased **venous tone** (sympathetic venoconstriction mobilising the splanchnic reservoir), the **skeletal-muscle pump**, the **respiratory pump** (inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, augmenting venous return), a longer diastole (bradycardia), and the **atrial kick**. Gravity/standing, venodilators (nitrates), hypovolaemia and tachycardia **lower** it.

Guyton framed this as **mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP ~7 mmHg)** - the pressure in the vasculature with no flow, set by volume and venous tone - driving blood back toward the right atrium. Venous return is proportional to **(MSFP - right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return**, so a *rising* RA pressure actually *reduces* venous return (the back-pressure opposes it).
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
[[figure:preload-venous-return]]

On a PV loop, **increasing preload widens the loop to the right** (higher EDV) and - with contractility and afterload unchanged - the end-systolic point stays on the same ESPVR, so **stroke volume increases** (Frank-Starling). This is pure length-dependent activation, not a change in contractility.

Clinical surrogates and normals: **PCWP 6-12 mmHg** (estimates LA pressure and hence LVEDP when there is no mitral obstruction), **CVP/RAP 2-6 mmHg**. PCWP rises in LV failure and volume overload; it is falsely high relative to LVEDP in mitral stenosis.

Note the "Starling" name appears twice and they are different: the **Frank-Starling** law relates *cardiac* stretch to force, whereas the **Starling forces** (capillary hydrostatic vs oncotic pressures) govern transcapillary fluid filtration and oedema.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Preload is the "tank" the heart draws from. Half of resuscitation, diuresis, nitrate therapy and the interpretation of wedge pressures is really about moving the ventricle along its Frank-Starling curve. Separating preload (stretch/volume) from the pressures we use to estimate it prevents the commonest reasoning errors in heart failure and shock.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Preload is a volume/stretch, not a pressure** - LVEDP only tracks it when compliance is normal. In a stiff ventricle (LVH, HFpEF) a high LVEDP/PCWP can coexist with a *normal or low* EDV.
- **PCWP overestimates LVEDP in mitral stenosis** (the obstruction holds LA pressure up).
- Do not confuse **Frank-Starling (cardiac)** with **Starling forces (capillary filtration)**.
- Giving fluids only helps if the ventricle is on the **steep** part of its Starling curve; on the flat part it just raises filling pressure and causes congestion.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Best clinical estimate of LV preload?" -> **PCWP** (then LVEDV on echo/ventriculography).
- A question that raises CVP and asks about venous return -> remember the **back-pressure effect lowers VR**.
- Nitroglycerin's main haemodynamic action -> **venodilation -> reduced preload**.
- A fluid-challenge/Starling-curve stem tests whether the patient is preload-responsive (steep part) vs congested (flat part).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Preload = **end-diastolic stretch** ~ LVEDV; clinical index = **PCWP (6-12 mmHg)**.
- **MSFP ~7 mmHg** is the x-intercept of the venous return curve.
- **Rising RA pressure lowers venous return** (it is the back-pressure).
- Venodilators (**nitrates**) and diuretics lower preload - the basis of relieving pulmonary congestion.
- The **atrial kick** is a preload contributor; losing it (AF) matters most in stiff/non-compliant ventricles.
- Inspiration **increases** right-heart venous return (and transiently splits S2).
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
This guide follows the ESC 2019 pathway that the PPDS exam is built on: **stable or unstable first**, then probability, D-dimer and CTPA, then **risk class**, which decides between home treatment, monitoring and reperfusion. The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline adds its own A-E categories; they are mapped below.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:pulmonary-embolism-algorithm]]

### Scores at the bedside
| Tool | Items | How it is used |
|---|---|---|
| sPESI (1 point each) | Age >80; cancer; chronic HF or chronic lung disease; HR ≥110; SBP <100; SaO2 <90% | 0 = low 30-day mortality; ≥1 = intermediate risk |
| YEARS | Clinical signs of DVT; haemoptysis; PE most likely diagnosis | 0 items: D-dimer <1000 ng/mL excludes; ≥1 item: D-dimer <500 excludes |
| PERC (all must be absent) | Age ≥50; HR ≥100; SaO2 <95%; haemoptysis; oestrogen; prior VTE; unilateral leg swelling; recent surgery/trauma | Only for very low gestalt probability; all negative = no testing |
| Age-adjusted D-dimer | Age x 10 µg/L after 50 years | Raises specificity in older patients (ESC 2019 IIa B) |
| Wells (two-level) | DVT signs 3; PE most likely 3; HR >100 1.5; immobilisation/surgery 1.5; prior VTE 1.5; haemoptysis 1; cancer 1 | >4 = PE likely -> CTPA; ≤4 = D-dimer first |
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### ESC 2019 early mortality risk classes
| Risk class | Haemodynamic instability | sPESI ≥1 or PESI III-V | RV dysfunction (TTE/CTPA) | Raised troponin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High | Yes | (+) | Yes | (+) |
| Intermediate-high | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Intermediate-low | No | Yes | One or none positive | One or none positive |
| Low | No | No | No (if assessed) | No (if assessed) |

### AHA/ACC 2026 PE Categories (in brief)
| Category | Meaning | Usual setting |
|---|---|---|
| A | Asymptomatic (incidental) PE | Outpatient |
| B | Symptomatic, low severity score (e.g. sPESI 0); B1 subsegmental, B2 more proximal | Early discharge generally |
| C (C1-C3) | Elevated severity score; C1 normal RV and biomarkers, C2 abnormal RV or biomarker, C3 both abnormal | Hospital; anticoagulation |
| D1 / D2 | Incipient failure: transient hypotension / normotensive shock (lactate, AKI) | Hospital; advanced therapy may be considered |
| E1 / E2 | Persistent hypotension with cardiogenic shock / refractory shock or arrest | Systemic thrombolysis (Class 1); catheter or surgical therapy reasonable; VA-ECMO reasonable in refractory shock |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
- **High risk**: UFH + systemic thrombolysis (ESC 2019 I B); surgical embolectomy (I C) or catheter-directed therapy (IIa C) if contraindicated or failed.
- **Intermediate-high**: anticoagulation, monitoring, **rescue** thrombolysis on deterioration (I B); routine primary thrombolysis not recommended (III B).
- **Intermediate-low**: anticoagulation in hospital.
- **Low**: DOAC; early discharge if Hestia/sPESI allow (IIa A).
- Parenteral choice: LMWH or fondaparinux over UFH, except in instability or planned reperfusion.
- Oral choice: DOAC over VKA (I A); VKA for antiphospholipid syndrome and when DOACs are contraindicated.
- Duration: ≥3 months for all; stop after a major transient risk factor; extended therapy if unprovoked or persistent risk factor.
- Follow-up: ask about dyspnoea and exercise limitation at every visit for at least 1 year to detect CTEPD/CTEPH (AHA/ACC 2026).
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: PE is the classic 'do not miss' cause of chest pain, syncope and shock, and the exam tests a single skill: matching the intensity of treatment to the risk class. Over-treating with thrombolysis kills through bleeding; under-treating high-risk PE kills through RV failure.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Sending an **unstable** patient to CT when bedside echo would decide (normal RV practically excludes PE as the cause of shock).
- Ordering D-dimer when clinical probability is **high** (a negative result does not exclude PE): go to CTPA.
- Using a fixed 500 cut-off in an 80-year-old (use **age x 10**).
- Calling sPESI 0 with RV dysfunction 'low risk': ESC 2019 classes it **intermediate-low**.
- Routine thrombolysis in intermediate-high risk (PEITHO: bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke outweigh benefit).
- Large fluid boluses in RV failure (worsens septal shift).
- DOACs in pregnancy or antiphospholipid syndrome.
- Using echo to diagnose PE in a stable patient (AHA/ACC 2026: do not use echo to confirm or exclude PE).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs, RV dilated with **McConnell sign** -> high-risk PE -> thrombolysis.
- ECG S1Q3T3, sinus tachycardia, new RBBB, T inversion V1-V4 -> RV strain.
- Normotensive PE with RV/LV ≥1 and raised troponin -> **intermediate-high**: anticoagulate and monitor, not routine thrombolysis.
- Pregnant woman with suspected PE -> pregnancy-adapted YEARS, LMWH.
- 'Which DOAC needs heparin lead-in?' -> **dabigatran and edoxaban**.
- Persistent dyspnoea 3 months after PE with mismatched perfusion defects -> **CTEPH** (V/Q scan is the screening test).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Instability definition: arrest, obstructive shock, or persistent hypotension (SBP <90 or drop ≥40 mmHg >15 min).
- RV dysfunction: RV/LV ≥1.0, TAPSE <16 mm.
- Intermediate-high = sPESI ≥1 + RV dysfunction + troponin.
- Thrombolysis: high risk (I B) and rescue (I B); not routine otherwise (III B).
- Alteplase 100 mg over 2 h.
- DOAC over VKA; LMWH over UFH unless unstable.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
The kidney, heart, brain, adrenal and blood vessels share one control system that defends **effective arterial blood volume** and **blood pressure**.
- **Volume-conserving, pressor arm**: the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)**, the **sympathetic nervous system (SNS)** and **ADH (vasopressin)**.
- **Volume-shedding, depressor arm**: the **natriuretic peptides** (ANP, BNP) and **pressure natriuresis** by the kidney.

Heart failure, hypertension, cirrhosis and most cardiovascular drugs are best understood as shifts of this balance.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### The cascade
1. **Angiotensinogen** (made by the liver) is cleaved by **renin** (from the juxtaglomerular, JG, cells of the afferent arteriole) to **angiotensin I**. Renin release is the **rate-limiting step**.
2. **Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)**, abundant on pulmonary vascular endothelium, converts Ang I to **angiotensin II**. ACE is the same enzyme as **kininase II**, so it also **breaks down bradykinin**.
3. Ang II acts mainly through **AT1 receptors**. AT2 receptors mediate broadly opposite effects (vasodilatation, antiproliferation). Tissue enzymes such as **chymase** can also make Ang II, one reason Ang II can partly recover during ACE inhibition.

[[figure:raas-cascade]]

### What releases renin
| Trigger | Sensor | Clinical examples |
|---|---|---|
| Low renal perfusion pressure | Baroreceptor in the afferent arteriole (JG cells) | Hypovolaemia, hypotension, low cardiac output, renal artery stenosis |
| Low NaCl delivery to the distal tubule | **Macula densa** | Volume depletion, low salt intake, **loop diuretics** (they block NKCC2 in the macula densa itself) |
| Sympathetic activity | **β1 receptors** on JG cells | Standing up, haemorrhage, heart failure |

Renin is **suppressed** by Ang II (short-loop negative feedback), ANP/BNP, high renal perfusion pressure, high distal NaCl and β-blockers.

### Angiotensin II (AT1) actions
- **Arteriolar vasoconstriction** -> raises SVR and blood pressure.
- Constricts the **efferent more than the afferent** arteriole -> keeps glomerular pressure and GFR up when renal perfusion falls.
- **Aldosterone** release from the adrenal zona glomerulosa.
- **Proximal tubular Na+ reabsorption** (Na+/H+ exchanger).
- **Thirst** and **ADH** release.
- Facilitates **sympathetic** outflow and noradrenaline release.
- **Trophic effects**: myocyte hypertrophy, fibroblast activation and fibrosis, vascular remodelling.

### Aldosterone
Binds mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) in the **principal cells** of the late distal tubule and collecting duct: more **ENaC** channels and Na+/K+-ATPase -> Na+ reabsorption and **K+ secretion**; intercalated cells secrete H+. Release is driven by Ang II and, independently, by **hyperkalaemia** (and ACTH). In the heart and vessels, MR activation promotes fibrosis. During long-term ACEi or ARB therapy aldosterone can drift back up (**aldosterone escape**), one rationale for adding an MRA.

### The counter-regulators and partners
- **Natriuretic peptides**: **ANP** from atrial myocytes (stretch); **BNP** mainly from ventricular myocytes (wall stress). Effects: natriuresis and diuresis (higher GFR, less collecting-duct Na+ reabsorption), vasodilatation, inhibition of renin, aldosterone and sympathetic tone. Removed by the clearance receptor (NPR-C) and degraded by **neprilysin**. The inactive fragment **NT-proBNP** is released in equal amounts with BNP but is **not a neprilysin substrate**.
- **ADH (vasopressin)**: released mainly by rising **plasma osmolality** (hypothalamic osmoreceptors). A large fall in effective arterial volume or pressure also releases it (**non-osmotic** release) and overrides osmolality. **V2** receptors in the collecting duct insert **aquaporin-2** -> free-water retention; **V1a** receptors cause vasoconstriction.
- **Sympathetic nervous system**: β1 -> renin release, tachycardia, inotropy; α1 -> renal and systemic vasoconstriction; increased proximal Na+ reabsorption.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
### Short-term vs long-term blood pressure control
- **Seconds**: the baroreflex adjusts HR, contractility and vascular tone; it resets within days, so it does not set long-term BP.
- **Minutes to hours**: RAAS and ADH add vasoconstriction and start retaining volume.
- **Days and beyond**: **pressure natriuresis** (Guyton's renal body-fluid feedback). A higher arterial pressure makes the kidney excrete more Na+ and water until volume and pressure fall back. Long-term BP is therefore set by the kidney's pressure-natriuresis curve; sustained hypertension needs that curve to shift to a higher pressure (for example by excess Ang II or aldosterone, or reduced nephron mass).

### Heart failure: a vicious circle
Low cardiac output -> underfilled arterial tree -> baroreceptors and JG cells read it as "hypovolaemia" -> SNS + RAAS + ADH -> vasoconstriction (more afterload), Na+ and water retention (more preload and congestion), hyponatraemia, myocyte death, hypertrophy and fibrosis -> worse ventricular function. Natriuretic peptides rise but cannot win. Guideline-directed therapy blocks the harmful arms and strengthens the helpful one.

### Pharmacology hooks: site of action vs effect
| Drug class (examples) | Site of action | Main effect | Exam points |
|---|---|---|---|
| ACE inhibitor (ramipril, enalapril) | ACE (kininase II) | ↓ Ang II and aldosterone; ↑ bradykinin; efferent dilatation | Dry cough and angioedema (bradykinin); hyperkalaemia; contraindicated in pregnancy |
| ARB (valsartan, candesartan) | AT1 receptor | As ACEi but no bradykinin rise; renin and Ang II rise | Much less cough; do not combine with an ACEi |
| Direct renin inhibitor (aliskiren) | Renin | ↓ Ang I formation | Do not combine with ACEi/ARB in diabetes |
| MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) | Mineralocorticoid receptor (kidney, heart) | Natriuresis, K+ retention, antifibrotic | Hyperkalaemia; gynaecomastia with spironolactone |
| ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) | Neprilysin + AT1 receptor | ↑ natriuretic peptides; AT1 blockade | Stop an ACEi **36 h** before (angioedema); BNP rises on therapy, so follow **NT-proBNP** |
| SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) | SGLT2 in the proximal tubule | Glycosuria and natriuresis; more NaCl at the macula densa -> afferent constriction -> ↓ glomerular pressure | Small early eGFR dip is expected; benefit in HF across the EF range and in CKD |
| β-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) | β1 receptors (JG cells, heart) | ↓ renin release; ↓ HR and contractility | Part of neurohormonal blockade in HFrEF |
| Loop diuretic (furosemide) | NKCC2, thick ascending limb and macula densa | Natriuresis | Stimulates renin release (macula densa senses "low NaCl") |
| Vasopressin antagonist (tolvaptan) | V2 receptor | Free-water excretion (aquaresis) | Hypervolaemic or euvolaemic hyponatraemia |

### Why ACEi and ARBs raise creatinine
Removing Ang II dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering glomerular pressure and GFR. A modest early rise in creatinine (commonly up to about 30%) is expected and reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure, not injury. With **bilateral renal artery stenosis** (or stenosis to a single kidney) GFR depends on efferent Ang II tone, and an ACEi/ARB can precipitate acute kidney injury.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Almost every drug that improves survival in HFrEF (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) works by restraining a neurohormonal system that began as a rescue mechanism and became the disease. Knowing where each hormone is made, what triggers it and what it does lets you predict drug effects, side effects (cough, hyperkalaemia, creatinine rise) and lab traps (BNP on ARNI) without memorising lists.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- On sacubitril/valsartan, a rising **BNP** may reflect neprilysin inhibition rather than worsening HF; use **NT-proBNP** to follow the patient.
- ARBs do not raise bradykinin, but **angioedema can still occur** (rarely); never start an ARNI within 36 h of the last ACEi dose.
- Loop diuretics **raise** renin; β-blockers **lower** it.
- Hyponatraemia in heart failure is usually **dilutional** (excess water from non-osmotic ADH); total body Na+ is increased, so salt loading is wrong.
- The early eGFR dip after an SGLT2 inhibitor or ACEi is haemodynamic and expected, not a reason to stop.
- Hyperkalaemia is the shared limitation of ACEi, ARB, ARNI and MRA, especially in CKD and diabetes.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Mechanism of ACE-inhibitor cough?" -> **bradykinin (and substance P) accumulation**.
- "Patient on sacubitril/valsartan, which marker to follow?" -> **NT-proBNP**.
- "Creatinine rises sharply after starting an ACEi in a hypertensive smoker with an abdominal bruit" -> **bilateral renal artery stenosis** (GFR depended on efferent Ang II).
- "Which drug acts at the proximal tubule and restores tubuloglomerular feedback?" -> **SGLT2 inhibitor**.
- "Hypokalaemic hypertension with suppressed renin" -> **primary hyperaldosteronism**.
- "Hormone released by atrial stretch" -> **ANP**; "by ventricular wall stress" -> **BNP**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Three renin triggers: **↓ renal perfusion pressure, ↓ NaCl at the macula densa, β1 sympathetic stimulation**.
- ACE = kininase II -> ACEi raise bradykinin -> **cough, angioedema**.
- Ang II constricts the **efferent > afferent** arteriole (GFR protection).
- Aldosterone: principal cells, ENaC, **Na+ in, K+ out**; also released by hyperkalaemia.
- ANP (atria, stretch) and BNP (ventricles, wall stress) are natriuretic and are degraded by **neprilysin**; NT-proBNP is not.
- ADH: osmotic release normally; **non-osmotic** release in HF and cirrhosis -> dilutional hyponatraemia.
- Long-term BP is set by **pressure natriuresis**, not the baroreflex.
- Primary hyperaldosteronism: **high aldosterone, low renin**. Renovascular hypertension: **high renin, high aldosterone**.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: RAAS and neurohormonal control of volume and blood pressure

sections.body:
This guide decides the first treatment for a tachycardia with a pulse: **is it unstable (shock it)? Is the QRS narrow or wide? Is it regular?** A wide regular tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
**VT vs SVT with aberrancy - clues favouring VT**

| Clue | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Prior MI or structural heart disease | VT most likely (strongest single clue) |
| AV dissociation | Diagnostic of VT |
| Fusion or capture beats | Diagnostic of VT |
| Precordial concordance (all positive or all negative) | Favours VT |
| QRS >160 ms, northwest axis | Favours VT |
| Identical QRS to known BBB in sinus rhythm | Favours SVT with aberrancy |

**Regular narrow-complex differential:** sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT (orthodromic), atrial tachycardia, atrial flutter with fixed block (rate ~150 suggests 2:1 flutter).
sections.title: Differential diagnosis

sections.body:
Three questions in order: stability, QRS width, regularity. Then use vagal manoeuvres and adenosine as both treatment and diagnostic test for regular narrow rhythms.

[[figure:regular-tachycardia-algorithm]]
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**Acute therapy and classes**

| Situation | Therapy | AHA 2025 | ESC 2019 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Any unstable tachycardia | Synchronized cardioversion | COR 1, B-NR | Class I |
| Regular narrow, stable | Vagal manoeuvres | COR 1, B-R | First-line |
| Regular narrow, stable | Adenosine (6 then 12 mg; ESC 6-18 mg) | COR 1, B-R | I B |
| Regular narrow, stable | IV diltiazem or verapamil | COR 2a, B-R | IIa |
| Regular narrow, stable | IV beta-blocker | No COR assigned | IIa |
| Stable, drugs fail | Synchronized cardioversion | COR 1, B-NR | Class I |
| Regular monomorphic WCT, stable | Adenosine (diagnostic/therapeutic) | COR 2b, B-NR | IIa C if no pre-excitation |
| Stable WCT / VT | Procainamide, amiodarone (or sotalol) | COR 2b, B-R | Procainamide IIa, amiodarone IIb |
| Any WCT | Verapamil or diltiazem | **COR 3: Harm, B-NR** | Avoid |
| Unstable, irregularly irregular or polymorphic WCT | Adenosine | **COR 3: Harm, C-LD** | Avoid |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body: The tachycardia algorithm is short, but the wrong turn (calling VT 'SVT') is lethal. Examiners test the safety rules: shock the unstable, assume VT when wide, and keep verapamil away from wide complexes.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Verapamil for 'SVT' that is actually VT** - haemodynamic collapse. Never give verapamil/diltiazem for a wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin.
- **Haemodynamic stability does not mean SVT.** Many VTs are well tolerated.
- **Adenosine in irregular wide tachycardia** (pre-excited AF) can precipitate VF.
- **Slow adenosine injection** through a distal cannula fails: rapid push with a flush, proximal vein.
- **A regular rate of exactly ~150** should make you look for flutter waves.
- **Treating sinus tachycardia** with cardioversion or adenosine - treat the cause.
- **Magnesium for every polymorphic VT.** It is for torsades (long QT); with a normal QT think ischaemia (AHA 2025: routine magnesium 3: No benefit).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Young woman, sudden palpitations, regular narrow QRS 190 bpm, BP 110/70 -> modified Valsalva -> adenosine.
- 65-year-old with prior anterior MI, regular broad QRS 170 bpm, BP 120/80 -> VT -> procainamide or amiodarone; cardioversion if it fails.
- Adenosine slows the ventricular rate and sawtooth waves appear -> atrial flutter.
- Broad, irregular, very fast QRS of varying shape -> pre-excited AF -> procainamide/DC cardioversion, no AV-nodal blockers.
- Torsades in a patient on a QT-prolonging drug -> IV magnesium.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Unstable = synchronized cardioversion** (unless polymorphic: defibrillate).
- **Narrow regular:** vagal -> adenosine -> CCB/beta-blocker -> cardioversion.
- **Wide regular:** VT until proven otherwise; procainamide preferred over amiodarone in ESC 2019 (PROCAMIO).
- **Never verapamil/diltiazem in WCT** (AHA 2025 3: Harm).
- Recurrent AVNRT/AVRT: catheter ablation is first-line long-term therapy (ESC 2019).
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: tachycardia with a pulse (narrow vs wide complex)

sections.body:
**Starling forces** are the hydrostatic and oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressures acting across the capillary wall. Their balance decides whether plasma water stays in the vessel or moves into the interstitium.

The **Starling equation** gives the net fluid flux (Jv) out of the capillary:

`Jv = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - σ(πc - πi)]`

- **Pc** - capillary hydrostatic pressure: pushes fluid **out**.
- **Pi** - interstitial hydrostatic pressure: about zero or slightly negative in loose tissue; when it rises it opposes filtration.
- **πc** - plasma oncotic pressure, mostly from **albumin** (about 25-28 mmHg): holds fluid **in**.
- **πi** - interstitial oncotic pressure: pulls fluid out.
- **Kf** - filtration coefficient (water permeability x surface area).
- **σ** - reflection coefficient for protein: 1 = wall impermeable to protein, 0 = freely permeable. High in skeletal-muscle capillaries, low in the leaky **liver sinusoids**.

**Oedema** is an excess of interstitial fluid. It develops when capillary filtration outruns **lymphatic** removal, and becomes clinically detectable (pitting) only after several litres have accumulated.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### Classic model vs the revised Starling principle
In the **classic model**, Pc falls along the capillary (about **35 mmHg at the arteriolar end to about 15 mmHg at the venular end**) while πc stays near **25 mmHg**. Fluid is filtered at the arteriolar end and mostly reabsorbed at the venular end; lymph returns the small remainder.

The **revised Starling principle** (glycocalyx model) refines this. The oncotic gradient that counts is across the endothelial **glycocalyx**, where the protein concentration just beneath it stays low. In most tissues at steady state there is **net filtration along the whole capillary** with little sustained venular reabsorption, so **lymph returns most of the filtrate**. Exam stems still use the classic numbers; the practical message is that the **lymphatics are the main safety valve**.

[[figure:capillary-starling]]

### Safety factors against oedema
Interstitial fluid does not pile up the moment filtration rises. Three buffers oppose it (Guyton):
1. **Low interstitial compliance** while Pi is negative: a little extra fluid raises Pi sharply and opposes further filtration.
2. **Increased lymph flow**: lymph flow can rise many-fold.
3. **Protein washout**: more filtrate dilutes interstitial protein, lowers πi and so restores the oncotic gradient.

Once Pi turns positive, interstitial compliance rises steeply, the gel swells and fluid accumulates freely. That is the point at which pitting oedema appears.

### Mechanisms of oedema
| Mechanism | Starling term | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure | ↑ Pc | Heart failure (venous congestion), DVT/venous obstruction, volume overload in renal failure, dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, pregnancy |
| Reduced plasma oncotic pressure | ↓ πc | Nephrotic syndrome (albumin loss), cirrhosis (less synthesis), malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy |
| Increased permeability | ↑ Kf, ↓ σ | Sepsis, burns, anaphylaxis, ARDS, local inflammation |
| Lymphatic obstruction | ↓ lymph removal | Lymphatic filariasis, malignant infiltration, lymph-node dissection or radiotherapy |
| Raised interstitial oncotic pressure | ↑ πi | Chronic lymphoedema (protein-rich fluid), myxoedema (glycosaminoglycans) |

### Cardiac, liver and kidney oedema: the kidney keeps the tap open
Starling forces explain *where* fluid goes; **renal Na+ and water retention** explains why the total amount keeps growing.
- **Heart failure**: high venous pressure raises Pc. The low output is also sensed as a low **effective arterial blood volume**, which activates the RAAS, the sympathetic system and ADH -> Na+ and water retention -> more congestion.
- **Cirrhosis**: portal (sinusoidal) hypertension drives ascites, low albumin lowers πc, and splanchnic arterial vasodilatation underfills the arterial tree -> RAAS, SNS and ADH -> Na+ and water retention.
- **Nephrotic syndrome**: two mechanisms coexist. **Underfill**: low πc moves fluid out, arterial volume falls, RAAS rises. **Overfill**: primary Na+ retention by the collecting duct even when blood volume is normal or high. Many adults show the overfill pattern.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
### Left vs right heart failure congestion
| | Left-sided failure | Right-sided failure |
|---|---|---|
| Pressure that rises | LA -> pulmonary venous and capillary pressure (PCWP) | RA -> systemic venous pressure (JVP/CVP) |
| Where the fluid goes | Lung interstitium, then the alveoli | Dependent tissues, liver, gut, peritoneal space |
| Symptoms | Exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, cough | Leg or sacral swelling, abdominal distension, right upper quadrant ache, early satiety |
| Signs | Basal crackles, interstitial or alveolar oedema on CXR | Raised JVP, hepatojugular reflux, tender hepatomegaly, ascites, pitting oedema |
| Commonest cause | Ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, valve disease | **Left heart failure** (via post-capillary pulmonary hypertension) |

Pleural effusions in heart failure are most typical when **both** systemic and pulmonary venous pressures are high (biventricular failure).

[[figure:heart-failure-congestion]]

### Why the lung stays dry for so long
Mean pulmonary capillary pressure is low (about 7 mmHg) while plasma oncotic pressure is about 25-28 mmHg, so the lung has a wide margin. The classic chest X-ray correlation with PCWP:
- **~13-18 mmHg** -> upper-lobe venous diversion
- **~18-25 mmHg** -> interstitial oedema (Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing)
- **>25 mmHg** -> alveolar oedema

In **chronic** heart failure, lymphatic drainage increases greatly, so patients tolerate wedge pressures that would flood the lungs of a patient with **acute** failure (acute MI, acute severe mitral regurgitation).

### Gravity decides the distribution
Hydrostatic pressure in dependent veins adds to Pc. Cardiac oedema therefore collects at the **ankles** in an ambulant patient and over the **sacrum** in a bed-bound one. Pitting means mobile interstitial water; chronic lymphoedema and myxoedema are typically **non-pitting** because the fluid is protein- or matrix-rich.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
The JVP is the bedside measure of whether Pc is high **because venous pressure is high**.
- **Oedema + raised JVP** -> right-sided or biventricular failure, volume overload (renal failure), constrictive pericarditis, severe tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension.
- **Oedema + normal JVP** -> look for low albumin (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition), a drug cause (dihydropyridine CCB), or a local cause (venous or lymphatic).
- **Unilateral** leg oedema is local (DVT, cellulitis, lymphatic obstruction) until proven otherwise; heart failure is bilateral.
sections.title: Jugular venous pulse (JVP)

sections.body: Every oedematous patient you will see - in heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, sepsis or filariasis - is a Starling-equation problem combined with a kidney that keeps retaining Na+. Naming which term has changed (Pc, πc, permeability or lymph) tells you the cause, predicts which treatment will work (diuretic, albumin, treating the leak, compression) and explains why the lungs and the legs behave so differently.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Starling forces** (capillary filtration) are not the **Frank-Starling** law (cardiac stretch -> force).
- Do not assume venular reabsorption returns the filtrate: in the revised model **lymph flow** does most of it.
- Low albumin plus oedema does not prove a cardiac cause, and heart failure does not need low albumin: **check the JVP**.
- Pulmonary oedema with a **normal PCWP** points to increased permeability (ARDS, sepsis), not to raised hydrostatic pressure. Classic ARDS definitions used PCWP ≤18 mmHg to exclude a cardiac cause.
- Amlodipine oedema is **not** fluid overload; doubling the diuretic is the wrong answer.
- A patient with chronic mitral stenosis and a PCWP of 25 mmHg may have clear lungs; an acute rise to the same value floods them.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Main Starling force behind oedema in nephrotic syndrome?" -> **↓ plasma oncotic pressure** (plus primary renal Na+ retention).
- "Mechanism of ankle oedema with amlodipine?" -> **precapillary arteriolar dilatation -> ↑ Pc**.
- Chronic, non-pitting leg swelling in a patient from an endemic area of Indonesia -> **lymphatic filariasis** (*Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*) -> lymphatic obstruction.
- Ascites with **SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL, protein ≥2.5 g/dL, raised JVP** -> cardiac ascites (right HF or constrictive pericarditis).
- **Kerley B lines** on CXR -> interstitial oedema, PCWP roughly 18-25 mmHg.
- Oedema + raised JVP + clear lungs -> right-sided failure (cor pulmonale, RV infarction, tricuspid disease, constriction).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- `Jv = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - σ(πc - πi)]`; albumin generates most of πc.
- The **lymphatics** return most of the filtrate; they are the main safety valve against oedema.
- Cardiac oedema = **raised Pc** plus **neurohormonal Na+ and water retention** (RAAS, SNS, ADH).
- **Dihydropyridine CCB oedema**: precapillary (arteriolar) dilatation without matching venular dilatation transmits more pressure to the capillary -> ↑ Pc. Diuretics help little; adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB (which also dilates the venous side) lessens it.
- Acute pulmonary oedema: interstitial at PCWP ~18-25 mmHg, alveolar above ~25 mmHg; chronic HF tolerates more because lymph flow adapts.
- **Cardiac ascites** (right heart failure, constriction): high serum-ascites albumin gradient (**SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL**) with **high ascitic protein (≥2.5 g/dL)**, because the leaky sinusoids pass protein. Cirrhotic ascites: high SAAG, low protein.
- Non-pitting oedema: lymphoedema (chronic), myxoedema.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
**Syncope** is transient loss of consciousness due to cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, short duration and spontaneous complete recovery. This guide decides: is it syncope, does the initial evaluation already give the diagnosis, and if not, **how risky is it** - which sets discharge, observation or admission and the next test.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
The initial evaluation is three things: **history (with a witness), examination with supine and standing BP, and a 12-lead ECG.** It gives the diagnosis in many patients. Everyone else is risk-stratified.

[[figure:syncope-algorithm]]
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**ESC 2018 risk features at initial evaluation (paraphrased from Table 6)**

| Domain | High risk (serious condition) | Low risk (benign) |
|---|---|---|
| Event | New chest discomfort, breathlessness, abdominal pain or headache; syncope during exertion or supine; sudden palpitations immediately followed by syncope | Typical reflex prodrome (light-headed, warm, sweating, nausea); after unpleasant sight/sound/smell/pain; prolonged standing or hot crowded place; during or after a meal; cough, micturition, defecation; head rotation; on standing up |
| Past history | Severe structural or coronary heart disease (HF, low LVEF, prior MI) | Long history of similar recurrent episodes; no structural heart disease |
| Examination | Unexplained SBP <90 mmHg; persistent bradycardia <40 bpm awake without training; undiagnosed systolic murmur; suggestion of GI bleeding | Normal examination |
| ECG (major) | Acute ischaemia; Mobitz II or third-degree AV block; slow AF <40 bpm; pauses >3 s awake; BBB, ventricular hypertrophy or Q waves; VT; device malfunction; type 1 Brugada; QTc >460 ms | Normal ECG |

Minor ECG features (high risk only when the history suggests arrhythmia): Mobitz I or long PR, mild sinus bradycardia 40-50 bpm, paroxysmal SVT/AF, pre-excitation, short QTc (<=340 ms), atypical Brugada, ARVC-type changes.
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
**Disposition and tests**

| Situation | Action | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Low risk | Discharge from ED, education (class I, B) | ESC 2018 |
| High risk | Early intensive evaluation in ED/syncope unit or admission (class I, B) | ESC 2018 |
| Neither | ED observation or syncope unit rather than admission (class I, B) | ESC 2018 |
| Orthostatic hypotension | SBP fall >=20 or DBP >=10 mmHg, or SBP <90 on standing | ESC 2018 |
| Carotid sinus massage | Age >40 with unexplained reflex-type syncope; positive = pause >3 s and/or SBP fall >50 mmHg | ESC 2018 |
| Echocardiography | Known or suspected structural heart disease | ESC 2018 |
| Exercise test | Syncope during or shortly after exertion | ESC 2018 |
| EP study | Unexplained syncope with bifascicular block; pace if HV >=70 ms | ESC 2018; ESC 2021 pacing |
| Implantable loop recorder | Recurrent unexplained syncope with high recurrence likelihood; high-risk after negative workup (class I) | ESC 2018 |
| Routine lab panels, brain imaging, carotid Doppler | Not useful without specific indication | ACC/AHA 2017 |
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Syncope questions reward a structured approach: decide whether it is syncope, use the three bedside tools, and then sort by risk. That structure prevents both missed cardiac syncope and needless admissions.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Brain CT and EEG for every faint** - low yield; ECG and standing BP are the key tests.
- **Myoclonic jerks = seizure** - brief jerks are common in syncope.
- **Exertional syncope labelled vasovagal** - syncope *during* exercise is cardiac until proven otherwise (AS, HCM, anomalous coronary, CPVT, LQT1).
- **Admitting every patient** - low-risk reflex syncope should go home; intermediate risk can be observed.
- **Holter for rare episodes** - only useful if events are frequent; use an ILR for infrequent recurrent syncope.
- **Pacing young vasovagal patients** - pacing is reserved for older patients (typically >40 y) with documented asystolic reflex syncope.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- 22-year-old faints at a blood draw after feeling warm and nauseous, normal ECG -> reflex syncope -> reassure, discharge.
- 75-year-old on three antihypertensives faints on standing, BP 140/80 -> 110/70 at 3 min -> orthostatic hypotension -> reduce drugs.
- Syncope while running, ejection systolic murmur louder with Valsalva -> HCM.
- Syncope with RBBB + left anterior fascicular block -> EPS; HV 80 ms -> pacemaker.
- Recurrent unexplained syncope, normal echo and ECG, Holter negative -> implantable loop recorder.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Three causes: **reflex** (most common), **orthostatic**, **cardiac** (worst prognosis).
- Initial evaluation = history + standing BP + ECG.
- High-risk markers: exertional or supine syncope, palpitations before syncope, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG.
- Disposition is risk-based: low -> home, high -> intensive evaluation/admit, neither -> observation/syncope unit.
- ILR has the highest diagnostic yield for infrequent recurrent unexplained syncope.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: syncope evaluation and disposition

sections.body:
A **stenotic valve** is a narrow orifice: to push the same stroke volume through a smaller area, blood must **accelerate**, and the energy for that comes from a **pressure drop** across the valve (the gradient). A **regurgitant valve** lets part of each stroke volume leak back through an orifice that should be closed.

Echocardiography measures **velocity** (Doppler) and **diameters**; the physics below converts them into **gradients**, **valve areas** and **regurgitant volumes**.

Normal valve areas: **aortic about 3-4 cm²**, **mitral about 4-6 cm²**.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### Bernoulli: velocity -> pressure gradient
At a stenosis almost all the pressure energy is converted to kinetic energy, so the full Bernoulli equation reduces to:

`ΔP (mmHg) = 4 x (v2² - v1²)`  (v in m/s)

When the proximal velocity v1 is small (about 1 m/s or less), it is ignored: **ΔP = 4v²** (the **simplified Bernoulli equation**).
- v = 3 m/s -> 36 mmHg; **v = 4 m/s -> 64 mmHg**; v = 5 m/s -> 100 mmHg.
- Include v1 when it is high (roughly ≥ 1.5 m/s): significant AR (high LVOT flow), subvalvular obstruction, serial stenoses.
- **Mean gradient** is the average of the instantaneous gradients over ejection, obtained by tracing the Doppler envelope. It is **not** 4 x (mean velocity)².

### Why the gradient depends on flow
Flow (Q) = area (A) x velocity (v), so v = Q/A and **ΔP is proportional to (Q/A)²**.
- At a fixed valve area, **doubling flow quadruples the gradient**; halving flow quarters it.
- High-flow states (exercise, pregnancy, fever, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, **coexisting AR**) make a moderate stenosis look severe by gradient.
- Low-flow states (LV dysfunction, small hypertrophied LV, severe MR, AF with fast rates) make a severe stenosis look moderate: **low-flow, low-gradient AS**.
- That is why severity is judged by **area and velocity/gradient together**, with flow (stroke volume index) always checked.

[[figure:gradient-flow-curves]]

### The continuity equation (conservation of mass)
The same stroke volume passes through the LVOT and then through the aortic valve:

`Area(LVOT) x VTI(LVOT) = AVA x VTI(AV)`, so `AVA = Area(LVOT) x VTI(LVOT) / VTI(AV)`

- `Area(LVOT) = π x (D/2)² = 0.785 x D²` (D = LVOT diameter in mid-systole).
- VTI = velocity-time integral (cm), the "stroke distance".
- **Dimensionless index (DVI)** = VTI(LVOT) / VTI(AV) (or the velocity ratio): needs no diameter; **< 0.25 indicates severe AS** (ASE/EACVI).

**Worked example**
1. LVOT diameter 2.0 cm -> LVOT area = 0.785 x 2.0² = **3.14 cm²**.
2. LVOT VTI 22 cm -> stroke volume = 3.14 x 22 = **69 mL**. With BSA 1.7 m², **SVi = 41 mL/m²** (normal flow, ≥ 35).
3. AV VTI 100 cm -> **AVA = 69 / 100 = 0.69 cm²**; indexed **0.41 cm²/m²**.
4. DVI = 22 / 100 = **0.22**.
5. AV peak velocity 4.6 m/s -> peak gradient = 4 x 4.6² = **85 mmHg**.
Conclusion: concordant **severe AS** with normal flow.

[[figure:continuity-equation]]

### Gorlin formula (catheter laboratory)
`AVA = CO / (HR x SEP x 44.3 x √mean gradient)`
- CO in mL/min, SEP = systolic ejection period (s/beat), 44.3 = empirical constant (for the mitral valve use the diastolic filling period and 37.7, i.e. 44.3 x 0.85).
- The core idea is the same as Bernoulli: **area = flow / √gradient**.
- **Hakki** shortcut: AVA ≈ CO (L/min) / √(peak-to-peak gradient).
- The formula is least reliable at **low flow**.

### Pressure half-time (PHT)
PHT is the time for the peak diastolic gradient to fall by half (velocity falls to peak / √2).
- **Mitral stenosis**: a tighter valve keeps the LA-LV gradient up longer, so PHT lengthens: **MVA ≈ 220 / PHT (ms)**. Unreliable immediately after balloon mitral commissurotomy, with significant AR, or when LA or LV compliance is abnormal.
- **Aortic regurgitation**: the bigger the leak, the faster aortic and LV diastolic pressures equalise, so PHT **shortens** (< 200 ms suggests severe; > 500 ms mild); a high LVEDP also shortens it.

### Regurgitant volume and EROA
- **Regurgitant volume** = total stroke volume through the leaking valve - forward stroke volume through a competent valve. **Regurgitant fraction** = RVol / total stroke volume.
- **PISA method**: flow converging on the orifice forms hemispheric shells. `EROA = 2πr² x Va / Vmax(regurgitant jet)`, where r is the PISA radius at the aliasing velocity Va. Then `RVol = EROA x VTI(regurgitant jet)`.
- PISA assumes a round orifice and a hemispheric shell; it **underestimates** the crescent-shaped orifice of secondary MR.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
### Pressure tracings in aortic stenosis
[[figure:as-pressure-tracings]]

- **Peak-to-peak gradient** (catheter): LV peak minus aortic peak. The two peaks do not occur at the same moment, so this is not a physiological instantaneous value.
- **Peak instantaneous gradient** (Doppler, 4v²): the largest gradient at any single moment; it is **always ≥ the peak-to-peak gradient**.
- **Mean gradient**: the average gap between the curves during ejection; Doppler and catheter values agree best here.
- The aortic pulse is **small and late (parvus et tardus)**: slow upstroke, delayed peak.
- **Pressure recovery**: downstream of the vena contracta some kinetic energy turns back into pressure, more so in a **small aorta (< 3 cm)**; Doppler then overestimates the net gradient compared with the catheter.

### Aortic stenosis severity
| Parameter | Mild | Moderate | Severe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peak velocity (m/s) | 2.0-2.9 | 3.0-3.9 | ≥ 4.0 |
| Mean gradient (mmHg) | < 20 | 20-39 | ≥ 40 |
| AVA (cm²) | > 1.5 | 1.0-1.5 | ≤ 1.0 (ESC: < 1.0) |
| Indexed AVA (cm²/m²) | - | - | ≤ 0.6 (ESC: < 0.6) |
| DVI (velocity or VTI ratio) | - | - | < 0.25 |

Velocity and gradient grades: ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021. AVA for mild and moderate and the DVI: ASE/EACVI echo recommendations. Normal AV peak velocity is < 2.0 m/s.

### Severe stenosis of the mitral valve and severe regurgitation
| Lesion | Severe criterion (ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021) |
|---|---|
| Mitral stenosis | MVA ≤ 1.5 cm² (clinically significant / severe) |
| Primary mitral regurgitation | EROA ≥ 0.40 cm², regurgitant volume ≥ 60 mL, regurgitant fraction ≥ 50%, vena contracta ≥ 0.7 cm |
| Aortic regurgitation | EROA ≥ 0.30 cm², regurgitant volume ≥ 60 mL, regurgitant fraction ≥ 50%, vena contracta > 0.6 cm |

### Low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis
Pattern: **AVA ≤ 1.0 cm²** but **mean gradient < 40 mmHg** and **Vmax < 4 m/s**; low flow = **SVi < 35 mL/m²**. First exclude measurement error (LVOT diameter underestimated, Doppler beam misaligned).
| Pattern | Setting | Confirm with | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classical LFLG | LVEF < 50%, SVi < 35 mL/m² | Low-dose dobutamine stress echo | **True severe**: mean gradient reaches ≥ 40 mmHg (Vmax ≥ 4 m/s) while AVA stays ≤ 1.0 cm². **Pseudo-severe**: AVA rises to > 1.0 cm² as flow rises. **No flow reserve** (SV rises < 20%): use the CT calcium score |
| Paradoxical LFLG | LVEF ≥ 50%, small thick-walled LV, SVi < 35 mL/m² (often elderly hypertensive women) | CT aortic valve calcium score | ESC 2021: severe AS **likely** with ≥ 2000 AU (men) or ≥ 1200 AU (women); **highly likely** with ≥ 3000 or ≥ 1600 AU |
| Normal-flow low-gradient | SVi ≥ 35 mL/m², AVA < 1.0 cm², mean gradient < 40 mmHg | Re-check the measurements | Usually moderate AS or a measurement error |

In classical LFLG a weak ventricle may not open a moderately diseased valve fully, so the AVA looks severe at rest; increasing flow separates true from pseudo-severe stenosis.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Every decision about valve intervention rests on numbers derived from a handful of physical laws: Bernoulli turns velocity into pressure, conservation of mass turns velocities into an area, and the flow dependence of gradients explains why the numbers sometimes disagree. Understanding the physics lets you spot the measurement error, recognise low-flow states and choose the right confirmatory test instead of memorising cut-offs blindly.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- The LVOT diameter is **squared**: a 10% error in D gives about a 20% error in AVA. Underestimating D is the commonest cause of a falsely small AVA.
- **Mean gradient ≠ 4 x (mean velocity)²**: it is the mean of 4v² over the envelope.
- High-output states and **coexisting AR** raise the gradient across a moderately stenotic valve; do not call it severe on the gradient alone.
- A Doppler gradient higher than the catheter gradient is expected (peak instantaneous vs peak-to-peak, pressure recovery); it is not automatically an error.
- PHT is **invalid** straight after balloon mitral commissurotomy, with significant AR or with abnormal LV compliance.
- In mitral stenosis **tachycardia** (exercise, AF, pregnancy) raises the gradient and LA pressure because diastole shortens and flow per second of diastole rises.
- An off-axis Doppler beam **underestimates** velocity and gradient (never overestimates).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Peak AV velocity 4.5 m/s, peak gradient?" -> 4 x 4.5² = **81 mmHg**.
- "LVOT 2.0 cm, LVOT VTI 20 cm, AV VTI 80 cm, AVA?" -> 3.14 x 20 / 80 = **0.79 cm²**.
- "MS with PHT 220 ms, MVA?" -> **1.0 cm²**.
- "AVA 0.8 cm², mean gradient 25 mmHg, EF 30%" -> classical LFLG -> **dobutamine stress echo**.
- "Same AVA but EF 65%, small LV, SVi 30 mL/m²" -> paradoxical LFLG -> **CT calcium score**.
- "Pregnant woman with moderate MS becomes breathless in the second trimester" -> higher flow and HR -> **higher transmitral gradient**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **ΔP = 4v²**: 4 m/s = 64 mmHg, 5 m/s = 100 mmHg.
- **Continuity**: `AVA = 0.785 x D² x VTI(LVOT) / VTI(AV)`.
- **ΔP is proportional to (flow / area)²**: gradients are flow-dependent, areas much less so.
- **Severe AS**: Vmax ≥ 4 m/s, mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, AVA ≤ 1.0 cm² (ESC < 1.0), AVAi ≤ 0.6 cm²/m², DVI < 0.25.
- **MVA ≈ 220 / PHT**; severe MS when MVA ≤ 1.5 cm².
- Gorlin constants: **44.3** (aortic), **37.7** (mitral).
- Doppler peak instantaneous gradient ≥ catheter peak-to-peak gradient; mean gradients agree best.
- LFLG AS with low EF -> **dobutamine stress echo**; with preserved EF -> **CT calcium score**.
